Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 47
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me, Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others

Vignette:
Kiet had always found solace in the great outdoors. As a park ranger, he spent his days hiking through forests and educating visitors about the importance of conservation. But it was during a family camping trip six years ago that his life took a drastic turn. His seven-year-old daughter, Mai, had suddenly fallen ill with a severe case of meningitis. Kiet remembered the feeling of panic as they rushed her to the hospital, the smell of antiseptic and sterile equipment filling his nostrils. The beeping of machines and hushed conversations of doctors and nurses still echoed in his mind. As he sat by Mai's bedside, watching her small body hooked up to tubes and wires, Kiet felt like he was losing control. He couldn't shake the feeling that he should have been able to protect her, that somehow this was all his fault. The hospital smell lingered on his clothes and in his car long after they returned home, a constant reminder of those harrowing days. Even now, when he caught a whiff of antiseptic or walked into a hospital, Kiet's mind would snap back to the ICU, his heart racing with anxiety. In the months that followed, Kiet became increasingly withdrawn. He found himself ruminating on what had happened, replaying every moment in his head and wondering if there was anything he could have done differently. His wife, Linh, tried to be supportive, but Kiet pushed her away, unable to shake the feeling of guilt and anger that had taken up residence inside him. He began to fixate on the doctors who had treated Mai, replaying their conversations in his head and imagining all the ways he could confront them about perceived mistakes. As a park ranger, Kiet was surrounded by people every day, but he started to dread interactions with visitors. He worried that someone would ask him about Mai's illness or bring up memories of the hospital, sending him spiraling back into darkness. He began to avoid leading group hikes and instead focused on solo projects, like trail maintenance and animal tracking. His colleagues noticed a change in him, but Kiet just brushed it off as stress. The smell of alcohol had also become a trigger for Kiet. One evening, while out with friends at a bar, he caught a whiff of whiskey on someone's breath and was instantly transported back to the hospital waiting room, where he'd sat with Linh, feeling helpless and scared. The sound of clinking glasses and laughter seemed to fade into the background as Kiet's mind began to replay the what-ifs. Lately, Kiet had started experiencing episodes of dizziness and lightheadedness. At first, he thought it was just exhaustion or dehydration, but deep down, he knew it was more than that. It was as if his body was trying to tell him something, reminding him of those chaotic days in the hospital when everything felt like it was spinning out of control. It wasn't until Mai's recent school project on family history that Kiet realized just how much his avoidance behaviors had cost him. As he watched her present about their ancestors and cultural traditions, he saw how his distance had affected not only his relationship with Linh but also his connection to his own heritage. He began to wonder if there was a way to break free from the cycle of rumination and guilt that had consumed him for so long. Kiet's dizziness had become more frequent, and Linh had finally convinced him to seek help. As he sat in the therapist's office, he felt a mix of emotions: fear of confronting the memories he'd been avoiding, hope that he might find some peace, and uncertainty about what lay ahead. He knew it wouldn't be easy, but Kiet was tired of living in the shadow of that hospital room.
